newsitem.title: PERU: Peru readies to tackle "El Nino" weather problems.
newsitem.headline: Peru readies to tackle "El Nino" weather problems.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori announced Wednesday the creation of a ministerial body to oversee measures to minimize the blow of a destructive weather system that could form late this year.

"It has the task of taking preventative steps to mitigate the effects that the El Nino phenomenon could produce. Even if it is not definitely forming, we must take action beforehand," Fujimori told reporters.
There are signs the El Nino weather system, which occurs every two to seven years, is starting to form but its strength will not be known until August, according to meteorologists.
The phenomenon has been nicknamed "El Nino," Spanish for "The Christ Child", because it usually occurs late in the year near Christmas.

El Nino, which can also affect crops and homes in the southern tier of the United States, northeast Brazil, southeastern Africa and the west Pacific, causes droughts in the south of Peru and heavy rainfalls in the country's north.
The system's strength can vary dramatically. In the late 1980s El Nino formed but was barely noticed in Peru, while in 1983 its widespread damage caused the economy to contract more than 12 percent.

If Peru experiences an El Nino this year, the effects would last about 18 months and likely be strongest from December to March, the Agriculture Ministry's planning director William Arteaga told Reuters. Cotton, sugar, potato and fruit crops would suffer most, he added.

Unions have also warned the climatic changes could drive fish catches away from Peru's waters, ruining small businesses in the industry. Fishing is Peru's second largest production sector after mining.

The new commission, made up of the presidency, transport and communications, agriculture and defense ministries, will have an initial budget of $19 million, Fujimori said on a visit to the northern department of Piura -- generally one the worst affected regions during an El Nino.
The government planned to focus its preventitive work improving agricultural infrastructure, including repairing irrigation channels and strengthening bridges, he said.
